source_text: Verum non hoc solum explanasse contentus aliud quoque ad confirmationem iustitiae huius a misericordiae operibus admovet argumentum et pronuntiat illis ipsis personis, quae sponte peccaverunt, si ad paenitentiam emendationemque confugerint, errores praeteritos non nocere. Iniquus - inquit - si convertat se ab iniquitatibus suis, quas fecit, et custodiat mandata mea, omnia delicta eius, quaecumque fecit, non erunt in memoria; in sua iustitia, quam fecit, vita vivet [n64] . Id est cum in hoc sim proposito clementiae, ut etiam propria indulgeam peccata correctis, qui potest fieri, ut imputem aliena nascentibus? Aut sinunt res, ut sit apud me rea innocentia, cum conditur, apud quem est efficax, si vel interpolata repetatur?
pass_a_gloss: But not content to have explained this alone he also moves another argument from the works of mercy to the confirmation of this justice and pronounces that to those very persons who have sinned of their own accord, if they have taken refuge in repentance and correction, past errors do not harm. The iniquitous, he says, if he turn himself from his iniquities which he has done, and keep my commands, all his offenses, whatever he has done, will not be in memory; in his justice which he has done he will live by life. That is: since I am in this purpose of clemency, that I even indulge own sins to those corrected, how can it happen that I impute others' to those being born? Or do things allow that innocence be defendant with me when it is founded, with whom it is efficacious if even interrupted it is sought again?

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Yet, not content to explain this alone, he brings in another argument from the works of mercy to confirm this justice. He declares that past errors do not harm even the very people who sinned voluntarily, if they turn to repentance and reform. ‘If the wicked person turns away from the iniquities he committed and keeps my commands, none of the offenses he committed shall be remembered. Through the justice he has practiced he shall surely live’ (Ezekiel 18:21–22). That is: Since my merciful purpose is to forgive even people’s own sins when they reform, how could I charge newborn children with someone else’s? Or could things be so arranged that innocence is guilty before me when it is created, although it has power with me when it is recovered after having been interrupted?
